name: Anaconda Control to Dead Orchard Control
summary: Anaconda Control is a front-headlock arm enclosure; Dead Orchard is a bottom-player leg triangle around both arms, so changing between them requires a separate guard exchange.
description: Anaconda Control is a front-headlock arm enclosure; Dead Orchard is a bottom-player leg triangle around both arms, so changing between them requires a separate guard exchange.
overview:
The attacker initially holds an Anaconda front headlock on top; Dead Orchard would require that player to reach a separate bottom rubber-guard configuration. Anaconda encloses the head and one arm with the arms. Dead Orchard encloses both arms with a high leg triangle from bottom guard. The reviewed sources establish these distinct configurations, not a direct top-player switch between them.

Confirm the front-headlock arm loop around the neck and one shoulder. Open the arm loop before either partner changes the body relationship. The intended Dead Orchard attacker must obtain a facing bottom-guard position; no direct transition is established here.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Nathan Orchard — Dead Orchard, part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoiB1D2WJwE); [Ben Eddy — the Zombie pummel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JzSxFvNA5Uo).

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): What does the starting arm loop contain?
flashcards.answer: The initial Anaconda uses the attacker's arms to enclose the neck and one opposing arm; Dead Orchard uses the legs.
flashcards.answer_line: The neck and one arm in the loop

plausible: Neck alone with both arms outside
The neck and both arms in the loop
trap: One upper arm with the neck outside

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): What releases the neck before changing seats?
flashcards.answer: Open the enclosing arms completely before changing the body relationship; merely easing the squeeze leaves the neck captured.
flashcards.answer_line: Unclasp and open the arm loop

plausible: Keep the clasp; soften the squeeze
Move the hand; retain the neck wrap
trap: Sit to guard with the loop linked

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): Which seat is needed for the new leg enclosure?
flashcards.answer: Dead Orchard requires a separate facing bottom-guard position. The sources do not demonstrate a direct switch from the top front headlock.

plausible: Top headlock over their shoulders
Side control beside their chest

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): In the new guard, how do you support the raised knee?
flashcards.answer: In the separate Mission Control phase, keep the hips close and support the raised knee rather than hauling the foot against it.
flashcards.answer_line: Bring hips close and hug the knee

plausible: Stay flat and pull the foot higher
Let the knee drift from the chest
trap: Hug the knee with the hips far away

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): What must the new leg triangle surround?
flashcards.answer: The Dead Orchard checkpoint is a high leg figure-four containing both opposing arms at the shoulder line.

plausible: The neck with only one arm inside
Forearms in; both shoulders outside
trap: The head with both shoulders outside

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): Where does the cooperative capture drill stop?
flashcards.answer: Check the both-arm enclosure without extending a captured elbow or compressing the partner's neck.
flashcards.answer_line: Both arms held; elbows left unloaded

plausible: Legs raised but figure-four open
Both arms held; one elbow extended

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): How do the two attacks differ in body orientation?
flashcards.answer: The initial attacker is above a front headlock. To become the Dead Orchard attacker, that player must separately obtain bottom guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Top headlock to facing bottom guard

plausible: Both attack above the shoulders
Both require chest-to-back contact
trap: A roll keeps the same attacking seat

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): How do the legs complete the destination control?
flashcards.answer: Anaconda uses an arm enclosure; Dead Orchard requires a newly established high leg enclosure around both arms.

plausible: High figure-four with one arm out
High shins with no figure-four

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): A neck is still fixed during the seat change; what first?
flashcards.answer: If the neck remains fixed, release the arm enclosure before turning or attempting the separate guard phase.
flashcards.answer_line: Open the neck loop before turning

plausible: Turn hips with the neck grip kept
Ease pressure; leave the arms linked
trap: Climb legs before undoing the wrap

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (attacker): What makes knee room while blocking chest pressure?
flashcards.answer: After the front headlock is released, inside frames and a small hip escape can create room for the knees before building high guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Inside frames plus lateral hip shift

plausible: Hip shift with both forearms outside
Pull knees up while staying flat

defender.name: Anaconda Control to Dead Orchard Control Defender
defender.description: Anaconda Control to Dead Orchard Control (defender): Treat a high leg triangle containing both your arms as an arm-lock threat even when the neck is not being choked. Keep the arms compact and avoid offering a straight arm while trying to force posture.
defender.overview:
The attacker initially holds an Anaconda front headlock on top; Dead Orchard would require that player to reach a separate bottom rubber-guard configuration. Anaconda encloses the head and one arm with the arms. Dead Orchard encloses both arms with a high leg triangle from bottom guard. The reviewed sources establish these distinct configurations, not a direct top-player switch between them.

Treat a high leg triangle containing both your arms as an arm-lock threat even when the neck is not being choked. Keep the arms compact and avoid offering a straight arm while trying to force posture. Maintain an early frame at the hip or thigh before the figure-four closes around the shoulders.

Work on opening the leg enclosure before withdrawing the shoulder and elbow together; stop if an arm is already loaded. Only raise posture after the shoulder line is free; a sudden pull can extend a captured elbow. Use a verbal tap or foot tap if both hands are trapped, and do not rely on pain to judge remaining range.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Protect the neck against the initial head-and-arm enclosure and address its grip as the first escape task. If the exchange later reaches Dead Orchard, the danger has changed to captured arms; keep a safe base and free each shoulder before moving away.
key_principles: Recognize both-arm capture: Treat a high leg triangle containing both your arms as an arm-lock threat even when the neck is not being choked.
Protect the elbows: Keep the arms compact and avoid offering a straight arm while trying to force posture.
Prevent the leg closure: Maintain an early frame at the hip or thigh before the figure-four closes around the shoulders.
Clear a shoulder safely: Work on opening the leg enclosure before withdrawing the shoulder and elbow together; stop if an arm is already loaded.
Recover base in stages: Only raise posture after the shoulder line is free; a sudden pull can extend a captured elbow.
Tap with any free signal: Use a verbal tap or foot tap if both hands are trapped, and do not rely on pain to judge remaining range.

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (defender): What can follow straightening an arm inside the new trap?
flashcards.answer: Once the exchange reaches Dead Orchard, both-arm capture exposes short arm locks even when the neck is not being choked.
flashcards.answer_line: Elbow extension into an arm lock

plausible: Only neck pressure from high legs
Shoulder escape as the elbow extends
trap: Wrist escape with the elbow unloaded

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (defender): How should your arms stay during the high-guard phase?
flashcards.answer: Keep the arms compact; Nathan Orchard's demonstration shows how a straightened arm assists the both-arm triangle and arm isolation.
flashcards.answer_line: Bent and close as you open the legs

plausible: Straight between the high legs
Reaching wide beyond the knees
trap: Pull wrist with its shoulder stuck

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (defender): Where can an early frame slow the new leg closure?
flashcards.answer: Before the high figure-four closes, a frame at the hip or thigh can preserve space. It is not a guaranteed escape after closure.
flashcards.answer_line: At the hip or thigh before closure

plausible: On the wrist without hip contact
Outside the thigh with elbow flared
trap: Straight arm on the mat by the hip

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (defender): When may you withdraw a captured shoulder and elbow?
flashcards.answer: Open the leg enclosure first, then withdraw the shoulder and elbow together through available space; stop if the arm is loaded.
flashcards.answer_line: After the high leg enclosure opens

plausible: Shoulder fixed while the wrist moves
As soon as the neck feels free
trap: While rolling through the leg lock

flashcards.question: Anaconda to Dead Orchard (defender): What must be free before you raise your chest?
flashcards.answer: Raise posture only after the shoulder line clears the high legs. Pulling upright with an arm still trapped can extend its elbow.
flashcards.answer_line: Shoulders clear of the high leg trap

plausible: Only the chin above their shin
Only one hand beyond their knee
trap: Only second leg down at the waist
